records.title: Implement Function Call Graph Analysis
records.body:
## Description
Trace function calls within contracts, build call graphs, identify entry points, detect unreachable/unused functions, and provide call chain analysis.

### Context & Why This Matters
Understanding function call patterns helps developers identify dead code, optimize hot paths, and verify that critical functions are reachable. This analysis is essential for contract auditing and optimization.

### Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Call graph generated showing function call relationships
- [ ] Entry points identified (functions without callers from contract start)
- [ ] Unused functions detected and listed
- [ ] Call depth calculated for each function
- [ ] Cyclic function calls detected
- [ ] Call chain output in both visual and structured formats

### Implementation Guidance
**Key files/modules:**
- Create `analyzer/src/callgraph.rs` - Call graph construction and analysis
- `analyzer/src/analyzer.rs` - Integrate call graph analysis phase
- `analyzer/src/metrics.rs` - Add call metrics structure
- `analyzer/src/report.rs` - Add call graph sections

**Suggested approach:**
1. Parse function definitions and their instruction sequences
2. Identify `call` instructions targeting other functions
3. Build directed graph of function calls
4. Compute entry points and reachability
5. Detect cycles using depth-first search
6. Generate metrics and visualizations

**Edge cases to consider:**
- Indirect calls through function pointers
- Tail call optimizations
- Call depth limits
- Mutually recursive functions

### Review Expectations
- Test coverage: 85%
- Documentation: Explain call graph algorithm
- PR must include: Unit tests for graph algorithms, integration tests, example call graphs
- Example: Show sample call graph with entry points and cycles

### Complexity
**150 points** — Requires graph algorithms and control flow analysis; moderate complexity with clear algorithmic foundation.

records.title: lean_single: `&(*boxed).array[i]` is a wrong address — silent, and it miscompiles the compiler
records.body:
## Summary

Taking a reference to an **aggregate element of an array inside a `Box`'d struct** and dereferencing it in a callee reads a **wrong address** under `lean_single`. No diagnostic, no crash — just a plausible-looking wrong number.

This matters more than a normal miscompile because `lean_single` is the seed that builds Madaros. Code with this shape anywhere in `self-hosted/` is silently wrong in the compiler that ships.

## Reproducer — 30 lines, no dependencies

`scripts/dev/ir-arena/repro_boxed_element_ref.sio` (on `refactor/ir-arena-soa`, reproduced below in full):

```sounio
struct Inner { tag: i64, bits: [i64; 8] }
struct Outer { n: i64, items: [Inner; 4] }

fn inner_sum(p: &Inner) -> i64 with Mut, Panic, Div {
    var t: i64 = 0
    var i: i64 = 0
    while i < 8 { t = t + (*p).bits[i as usize]; i = i + 1 }
    t
}

fn main() -> i64 with IO, Alloc, Mut, Panic, Div {
    var seed = Outer { n: 0, items: [Inner { tag: 0, bits: [0; 8] }; 4] }
    var slot = seed.items[2 as usize]
    var k: i64 = 0
    while k < 5 { slot.bits[k as usize] = 1; k = k + 1 }
    seed.items[2 as usize] = slot
    var ob = Box::new(seed)
    var hoisted = (*ob).items[2 as usize]
    print("hoisted=")
    print_int(inner_sum(&hoisted))
    print(" inplace=")
    print_int(inner_sum(&(*ob).items[2 as usize]))
    print("\n")
    0
}
```

```
$ ./bin/souc-lean-single-x86_64 repro_boxed_element_ref.sio out.elf && ./out.elf
hoisted=5 inplace=22499901309144
```

Both should be `5`. The second value varies per run — it is a pointer-shaped garbage read.

## The shape, narrowly

Three things that are **fine**, established by ablation:

- reading a **scalar** field in place through the `Box` — a fuller version of this program reads `tag_inplace=77` correctly
- the same program **without the `Box`** — prints `5` and `5`
- a by-value struct copy of the aggregate — a known 8-bit pattern survives it intact

What breaks is specifically: **`&` into an array element of a boxed aggregate, dereferenced in a callee.**

Workaround, one line, at every site:

```sounio
var el = (*boxed).items[i as usize]
f(&el)                                  // correct
f(&(*boxed).items[i as usize])          // garbage
```

## How it was found, and what it cost

On `refactor/ir-arena-soa` (#1649), a probe counting bits in an `[i64; 64]` field per function:

| | `live_at_codegen` |
|---|---|
| `ir_float_bits_get(&(*module).functions[i], r)` | 4003 / 4643 / 4963 — varied per run |
| hoisted to a local first | **8 / 8 / 8 — exactly the write count** |

Same binary, same probe, one line apart.

It also explains a fix already on that branch whose mechanism was recorded as unproven: `ir_module_seal_functions` sealed **0 of 7** regions and reported success, until the element was hoisted out of `(*module).functions[i].region`. The hazard is the reference, not sealing.

Before finding it I produced and killed three wrong diagnoses off the bad instrument — "the module is born dirty", "`Box::new` returns uninitialised memory", "the function slot is recycled memory". Each was falsified by measurement, but each cost a build cycle, and the second was nearly filed as a bug against `main`.

## Candidate sites in `self-hosted/` on `main`

Grep for address-of into a pointer-receiver array element:

- `self-hosted/compiler/pkg/lock.sio:217` — `let e = &(*lock).entries[i as usize]`
- `self-hosted/compiler/pkg/lock.sio:364` — same
- `self-hosted/compiler/pkg/registry_client.sio:430` — `registry_print_package(&(*r).packages[i as usize])`

These are off the IR path, so nothing here claims they currently produce a wrong build — they are where to look first. What the reproducer establishes is that the shape is unsound, so **no site of it can be assumed correct**.

## Acceptance

1. The reproducer prints `hoisted=5 inplace=5` under `lean_single`.
2. Any site of the shape in `self-hosted/` is either fixed or shown not to be reachable.
3. Ideally a gate rejecting new `&(*ptr).field[i]` where the element type is an aggregate — the failure is silent and returns plausible values, so review will not catch it.

## Separate observation, not this bug

`Box` in a **user program** under `madaros --native-v2-compile` segfaults on a plain field read: `Box::new(make())` then `print_int((*a).n)`, with `Flat { n: i64, xs: [i64; 32] }`, gives rc=139 with a compiler built from `origin/main`. That is a different path and probably a different defect; noting it because it is what blocked the first reproduction attempt.

Refs #1649, #1655, #1669

records.title: Improvement: add a conditional decision-requirements pass to SDD intake
records.body:
*The engine opened this item itself — you didn't create it.*

**What this is.** Add a conditional DMN-informed decision-requirements branch to the product-design (SDD) intake so decision-heavy capabilities expose missing rules, inputs, authorities, dependencies, and outcomes before the operator settles their specification—without imposing full DMN on every product.

**Problem.** The full-by-default intake established by #553, #570, and #574 lays out capability shape, authors behavior and acceptance criteria, checks form and traceability, and leaves correctness to the operator and advisory reviews. It has no explicit decision-requirements pass. For policy- or rule-heavy capabilities, a plausible behavior description can therefore reach acceptance criteria before the intake has systematically exposed the decisions being made, their required data, governing knowledge, dependent decisions, conflicting or missing rules, defaults, and failure behavior.

DMN is deliberately narrower than general requirements engineering: it precisely models business decisions and business rules. Making a conformant DMN model mandatory for every capability would add notation, tooling, and lifecycle cost where no decision service exists, while still failing to cover actors, workflows, state, quality attributes, security, accessibility, operations, migration, or recovery. The useful change is a progressive decision lens inside SDD, not replacement of SDD by DMN.

**Required boundary.**

- Screen each capability in plain language for repeatable, rule-governed decisions with identifiable inputs and outcomes. Record a minimal disposition so the lens is not silently skipped.
- If none exist, leave the normal SDD path unchanged.
- If they exist, begin with decision-requirements discovery: the decision and possible outcomes, input data and its source, knowledge or policy authority, dependent decisions, unresolved rules, representative examples, edge/default behavior, and failure/degraded behavior. A readable DRD-style view may support this level, but conformant XML or an execution engine is not required.
- Escalate to decision tables only for multi-condition logic that benefits from unambiguous rule coverage.
- Escalate to conformant executable DMN/FEEL only when executable rules, interchange, automated validation, or a business-editable decision service is itself an explicit product requirement.
- Use the decision model to strengthen only decision-related behavior and acceptance criteria. The rest of SDD remains responsible for the full product description.
- Preserve operator authority: pre-settle checks may enforce presence, shape, mapping, and disclosed unresolved items, but must never claim the decisions or the overall design are correct.

**Planning provenance.** Before finalizing the build plan, recall Engine session `01a02560-62e8-7302-929a-4b815acb910a`, anchor `1`, radius `6`. It contains the operator's originating DMN question, the current SDD-module and #553/#570/#574 inspection, the OMG scope analysis, and the progressive three-level recommendation. Treat that session as design rationale; this Issue is the tracked outcome.

**What happens next.** Implement this as an additive branch between capability-shape confirmation and finalization of decision-related acceptance criteria.

**Build outcomes.**

- Add the plain-language decision screen and minimal disposition to the intake and appropriate scaffold, without requiring the operator to know DMN vocabulary.
- For an applicable capability, create a repo-native readable decision-requirements artifact or bounded capability section covering decisions, outcomes, inputs, knowledge authorities, dependencies, unresolved rules, examples, edge/default paths, and failure/degraded behavior. Keep one canonical home rather than duplicating it across specification artifacts.
- Let newly discovered decisions or dependencies loop back to capability-shape confirmation when they reveal a missing product piece.
- Map decision outputs and rules to the capability's behavior and acceptance criteria; map decision-related acceptance criteria back to the relevant decision, rule, and planned evidence.
- Before settle, show a decision-closure report that makes missing inputs or authorities, unresolved conflicts, dependency cycles, and uncovered outcome/default/failure paths visible to the operator. It advises; the operator still decides whether to settle.
- Add mechanical form and traceability checks with biting negative fixtures. Every result must state the existing honesty bound: structure and mapping were checked, not semantic correctness or whole-spec completeness.
- Cover at least four demonstrations: a non-decision capability that incurs only the minimal screen; a decision-rich capability using requirements discovery only; multi-condition rules using decision tables; and an explicitly opted-in executable DMN case.
- Update operator guidance and generated provider projections through their canonical sources.

**Non-goals and safeguards.**

- Do not require full DMN, FEEL, XML, a modeler, or an execution dependency for ordinary SDD intake.
- Do not use DMN to represent architectural trade-offs or product-design decisions; those remain in the specification's decision context and ADR path.
- Do not claim that DMN proves the entire requirements set correct or complete.
- Do not weaken the full structured SDD default or its current form, review, settle, and change-confirmation flow.
- If normative executable support is introduced, target the current formal OMG version (DMN 1.5) and treat any later-version migration as a separate deliberate compatibility decision.

**More detail.**
- [OMG — Decision Model and Notation](https://www.omg.org/dmn/)
- [OMG — formal DMN 1.5 specification](https://www.omg.org/spec/DMN/1.5)
- [Issue #553 — structured SDD intake is the default](https://github.com/StarshipSuperjam/engine-template/issues/553)
- [PR #570 — full checked structured description by defa

records.title: chore(agent-tooling): optimize Claude, Codex, and Orca context usage
records.body:
## Summary

Optimize the repository's existing Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Orca setup to reduce duplicated context, avoid overlapping plugins and workflows, improve cross-agent memory, and measure whether changes actually reduce token usage without lowering implementation quality.

Sandcastle is explicitly out of scope. Orca remains the sole owner of feature coordination, worktrees, Dispatches, and durable workflow state.

## Current state

The initial audit found:

- Root `AGENTS.md` is canonical and currently about 94 lines.
- Root `CLAUDE.md` is about 75 lines and repeats commands, architecture, messaging, and release guidance already represented in the `AGENTS.md` hierarchy.
- `src/services/AGENTS.md` is about 465 lines and contains both invariants and detailed procedures.
- Claude currently has these plugins enabled: Superpowers, Microsoft Docs, TypeScript LSP, C# LSP, Security Guidance, Playwright, Frontend Design, GitHub, and Claude HUD.
- Codex has Orca lifecycle hooks configured, but no shared repository-specific MCP stack was identified.
- The repository already contains dedicated Teck planner, plan-reviewer, executor, code-reviewer, QA, direct-worktree, and feature-flow skills.

## Goals

- Reduce always-loaded instruction tokens.
- Keep one canonical source for repository rules.
- Load detailed procedures only when relevant.
- Prevent generic plugins from conflicting with the Teck Orca lifecycle.
- Provide useful, governed memory across Claude and Codex.
- Use a small, intentional shared MCP set.
- Measure token, latency, and quality changes before and after rollout.

## Target architecture

```text
AGENTS.md tree
  Stable repository rules and invariants

Teck skills
  Task-specific procedures and role workflows

Orca
  Coordination, worktrees, Dispatches, and workflow state

Optional AgentMemory
  Cross-session discoveries, corrections, and decisions

Small MCP set
  External documentation and services

Hooks and CI
  Deterministic enforcement
```

## Proposed work

### 1. Deduplicate Claude instructions

Reduce `CLAUDE.md` to a small Claude-specific adapter that imports the canonical root instructions:

```md
# Claude Code

@AGENTS.md

The AGENTS.md hierarchy is canonical. Before changing a file, read the
nearest applicable AGENTS.md.

Use Orca for all parent-feature coordination and worktree lifecycle.
Do not start a competing orchestration system.

## Claude-specific guidance

Use the C# and TypeScript language servers when working in those languages.
```

Confirm that all important content currently unique to `CLAUDE.md` is already present in the applicable `AGENTS.md`, moved there, or retained as genuinely Claude-specific guidance.

### 2. Audit and rationalize Claude plugins

| Plugin | Proposed treatment | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| C# LSP | Keep | High-value .NET navigation |
| TypeScript LSP | Keep | High-value TypeScript navigation |
| Claude HUD | Keep | Token and context visibility |
| Microsoft Docs | Keep or task-scope | Useful for .NET and Aspire |
| Playwright | Task-scope | Relevant to browser/frontend work |
| Frontend Design | Task-scope | Not relevant to backend work |
| Security Guidance | Task-scope | Relevant to security-sensitive work |
| GitHub | Review for duplication | Orca and `gh` may already cover the need |
| Superpowers | Disable for Teck feature flow unless proven compatible | Overlaps with planning, delegation, worktree, and lifecycle rules owned by Orca |

Document the final decision and how task-specific plugins should be activated.

### 3. Refactor large procedural instructions into shared skills

Review the larger `AGENTS.md` files, especially `src/services/AGENTS.md`, and separate short invariants, task-specific procedures, and long-form references.

Candidate skills:

- `teck-dotnet-service-scaffold`
- `teck-ef-migration`
- `teck-messaging`
- `teck-multi-tenancy`
- `teck-endpoint-pattern`
- `teck-container-publish`
- `teck-frontend-api-integration`

Keep mandatory rules in the nearest `AGENTS.md`. Move workflows, examples, validation commands, and troubleshooting into progressively loaded skills or references. Ensure the layout works for both native Claude Code and native Codex CLI without divergent sources.

### 4. Establish a measurement baseline

Across a representative set of issues, record where available:

- input, cache-read/cache-creation, and output tokens;
- tool-call and failed-tool-call counts;
- context compactions;
- wall-clock duration;
- human corrections;
- reviewer findings;
- rework after review.

Use a lightweight format that does not expose prompts, source code, credentials, or customer data.

### 5. Pilot shared AgentMemory

Evaluate https://github.com/rohitg00/agentmemory as a shared Claude/Codex memory layer.

Initially expose only recall/search, explicit remember/save, recap, correction/supersession, and forget/delete.

Store architectural decisions not yet formalized, failed approaches and causes, environment discoveries, repeated corrections/preferences, and concise handoffs.

Do not store secrets, full tool outputs/build logs, source files, customer/production data, temporary failures, facts cheaply discoverable from the repository, acceptance criteria, or authoritative workflow state.

Requirements:

- Pin a reviewed version instead of continuously using `latest`.
- Keep the service local by default; authenticate it if reachable beyond localhost.
- Define repository namespacing, retention, deletion, correction, and stale-memory handling.
- Restrict exposed MCP tools.
- Do not initially process every `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` event because Orca already uses lifecycle hooks.
- Audit memories before enabling automatic capture or retrieval.
- Compare the pilot with the baseline before retaining it.

### 6. Define a minimal shared MCP policy

Prefer no more than three generally enabled servers. Candidates are AgentMemory, targeted documentation retrieval such as Context7, and GitHub only when it adds capab

records.title: Optimize File/Folder Access Resolution Using Permission Scopes
records.body:
Summary

Our current file/folder authorization can require recursively walking the folder hierarchy to determine whether a user has access to an item.

PostgreSQL supports recursive CTEs specifically for hierarchical/tree data, but because access checks are a frequent operation, we should investigate whether our sharing constraints allow us to replace recursive permission resolution with indexed lookups.

The important current constraint is:

A Project is the root ownership boundary.
Only folders directly underneath the project root can be shared.
Everything below such a folder inherits that folder's sharing/access context.

This means an item should only need to resolve access through one of two paths:

1. User → Owning Project → Item

OR

2. User / Project → Shared Scope → Item

Instead of resolving permissions recursively through:

Item → Parent → Parent → ... → Project
Proposed Architecture

Separate the filesystem hierarchy from the authorization hierarchy.

Each file/folder would store its authorization context directly:

Item
----
id
parent_id
owner_project_id
access_scope_id

Where:

owner_project_id identifies the project that owns the content.
access_scope_id identifies the permission boundary the item inherits from.

Possible scope model:

AccessScope
-----------
id
owner_project_id
root_folder_id     nullable
kind               PROJECT | FOLDER

Every project has a project scope, while each shareable root-level folder can have its own folder scope.

All descendants of a shared root folder would carry the same access_scope_id.

This resembles the permission scope model used by SharePoint: descendants normally inherit permissions, while a folder with unique permissions forms a new permission scope shared by its descendants. Microsoft specifically recommends sharing folders rather than individually creating permission scopes for large numbers of files.

Access Grants

Permissions could be represented separately from the content tree:

AccessGrant
-----------
scope_id
principal_type
principal_id
role

A principal could initially be:

USER
PROJECT

and potentially later:

GROUP

Example:

Scope Folder-X
    Project B → READ
    User 123  → WRITE
    User 456  → ADMIN

This follows the same general relationship-based authorization principle used by systems such as OpenFGA, where permissions on a parent folder can determine permissions on its child documents.

Proposed Access Resolution

An item lookup could become conceptually:

can_access(user, item, permission) =
    has_project_permission(
        user,
        item.owner_project_id,
        permission,
    )
    OR
    has_scope_permission(
        user,
        item.access_scope_id,
        permission,
    )

The important part is that determining access would no longer require walking item.parent recursively.

The main lookup paths could instead be supported by indexes such as:

Item(owner_project_id)
Item(access_scope_id)

ProjectMembership(user_id, project_id)

AccessGrant(scope_id, principal_type, principal_id)
Shared Folders Between Projects

Sharing should preferably not change ownership or create multiple filesystem parents.

For example:

Project A
└── Folder X     ← owned here

Project B
└── Shared Folder X

Internally:

Folder X
owner_project_id = Project A
access_scope_id   = Scope X

and:

AccessGrant
scope      = Scope X
principal  = Project B
role       = READ

If necessary, a separate mount/reference entity could control where the shared folder appears:

ProjectMount
------------
project_id
scope_id
display_name

This keeps:

Ownership
Filesystem hierarchy
Authorization
UI/project mounting

as separate concepts.

Permission Model

Initial roles could be:

READ
WRITE
ADMIN

with:

ADMIN → WRITE → READ

For the first implementation this could be represented as hierarchical roles.

However, before finalizing the model we should decide whether future permissions need to be more granular, for example:

READ
WRITE
DELETE
SHARE
MANAGE_METADATA
MANAGE_PERMISSIONS

If that is likely, role → permission mappings may be preferable to hard-coded numeric permission levels.

Important Invariant

All descendants underneath a shareable root folder should have the same:

owner_project_id
access_scope_id

Changing/moving a subtree into another authorization scope would therefore require updating those values for its descendants.

This deliberately trades some cost on relatively uncommon move/share operations for simpler and potentially much faster read/access checks.

This needs benchmarking rather than assuming it is automatically faster.

Decisions Required Before Writing the Full Specification

We need to agree on the following design questions:

What is a principal?
User only?
User + Project?
Groups/Teams in the future?
How do project permissions interact with shared-folder permissions?
Does project membership always give access to everything owned by that project?
Can folder permissions ever restrict project members?
Do we support DENY permissions?
Recommendation for the initial design: positive grants only.
Adding explicit DENY introduces precedence rules between project, folder, user and group permissions.
What permissions do we require?
READ / WRITE / ADMIN
or granular capabilities?
How does sharing with another project work?
Does every member of the receiving project inherit the grant?
Can the receiving project grant different permissions to its own members?
What happens when content is moved between root scopes?
Synchronous update?
Background/batched update for very large trees?
Restrictions while the move is occurring?
What happens when a share is revoked?
Immediate access removal?
Cache invalidation requirements?
Audit requirements?
Should shared folders use a mount/reference model?
Recommended so content retains exactly one owner and filesystem parent.
Where is authorization enforced?
Django application/service layer?
PostgreSQL Row-Level Security as an additional safeguard?
PostgreSQL RLS can restrict SELECT, INSERT,

records.title: Attach comparable fare quotes to CTDF journey-plan results
records.body:
Parent feature: #158

## Problem

Fare data becomes a user feature only when it is attached to concrete journey choices. Quote work must remain bounded so fare providers do not make journey planning unreliable.

## Scope

- Quote completed `JourneyPlan` results server-side after route search.
- Add an opt-in `include_fares` planner parameter and bounded quote concurrency/time budget.
- Return fare summary, alternatives, certainty, availability, expiry and provider on each plan.
- Compare or rank by price only when currencies, passenger assumptions and certainty are compatible.
- Preserve the existing planner result when fare providers time out or cannot cover an itinerary.
- Make explicit ticket boundaries visible for genuinely split fare results.
- Add internal hooks for future cost-aware search without adding fare state to the planner label algorithm in this issue.
- Include fare-data versions in planner-cache invalidation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Planner results remain available when every fare provider fails.
- [ ] Local, TfL and National Rail fixture plans receive normalized summaries.
- [ ] Incomparable currencies or certainty levels are not silently ordered as cheapest.
- [ ] Quote concurrency and timeout tests prevent unbounded provider calls.
- [ ] Provider provenance and expiry survive API serialization.
- [ ] The non-fare planner response remains backward compatible when fares are not requested.
- [ ] Metrics distinguish unquoted, unavailable, partial, computed and authoritative plans.

## Dependencies

- #180
- #170
- #181
- #184

[REVIEW] rbac-design: add ReBAC graph cycle deny-edge handling gates
records.body:
## Skill Being Reviewed
**Skill name:** `rbac-design`
**Skill path:** `skills/identity/rbac-design/`

## False Positive Analysis
Relationship-based access can be safe when graph traversal has bounded depth, deterministic conflict resolution, and explicit deny edges that override grants.

## Coverage Gaps
Authorization reviews often check role names but miss graph behavior. Cycles, inherited group edges, or deny/grant conflicts can produce access that the policy author did not intend.

## Edge Cases
- User inherits access through cyclic team membership.
- Deny edge exists at resource level but grant edge exists at parent level.
- Cached graph result survives relationship removal.

## Remediation Quality
- Require cycle detection, max traversal depth, and conflict ordering.
- Require deny-before-grant tests for relationship policies.
- Flag unbounded graph expansion and stale decision caches.

## Comparison to Other Tools
Policy engines model relations; this review gate checks whether design evidence covers failure modes.

## Overall Assessment
Add ReBAC cycle and deny-edge gates so RBAC reviews cover graph authorization systems.
